lessons.title: Trie Structure and Purpose
lessons.concept: A trie (prefix tree) is a tree-like data structure used to store strings where each node represents a character/prefix. Paths from root to nodes form prefixes of stored strings. Tries are efficient for prefix-based operations like search, autocomplete, and dictionary lookups.
lessons.formula: Each edge/child corresponds to a character; a node may mark end-of-word. Search/insert/prefix-check time: O(L) where L is length of the string/prefix.
lessons.worked_example: Storing 'cat', 'car', 'dog': root branches 'c' and 'd'; under 'c' branch 'a', then 't' (end of cat) and 'r' (end of car); under 'd' -> 'o' -> 'g' (end of dog). Prefix 'ca' is found by traversing c,a.
mistakes: Confusing trie with binary search tree
Assuming trie stores full strings only at leaves (end markers can be on any node)
Ignoring memory overhead of many child pointers/references

lessons.title: Insert, Search, and Prefix Operations
lessons.concept: Insert: traverse/create nodes for each character of the word and mark the final node as end-of-word. Search: traverse characters; if path breaks return not found, else return true only if final node is marked end-of-word. Prefix search (startsWith): similar to search but success if path exists regardless of end marker.
lessons.formula: Insert(word): for ch in word create child if missing, move; mark end. Search(word): traverse all chars and check end marker. StartsWith(prefix): traverse all chars.
lessons.worked_example: After inserting 'apple', search('apple')=true, search('app')=false (unless inserted), startsWith('app')=true.
mistakes: Returning true for prefix search when end-of-word is required
Not marking end-of-word, causing false positives for shorter prefixes as words
lessons.provenance: Authored original lesson; not scraped. Requires independent verification before TRUSTED promotion.

lessons.title: Applications and Complexity
lessons.concept: Tries are used in autocomplete, spell checkers, IP routing (variants), and prefix matching. They offer predictable O(L) operations independent of number of stored keys (aside from traversal), but can use significant memory. Variants like compressed tries/radix trees reduce space.
lessons.formula: Time: O(L) per operation. Space: depends on alphabet size and shared prefixes; worst case can be high for many non-sharing strings.
lessons.worked_example: Autocomplete for prefix 'pro': traverse 'p','r','o' in trie, then collect all words in that subtree as suggestions.
mistakes: Assuming trie is always more space-efficient than hash table
Using trie when simple hash set lookup suffices and prefixes not needed
Not considering alphabet size impact on node structure
